- Boutique is used in hundreds of apps, and I thoroughly test every API in my app Plinky. (Which I highly recommend downloading and maybe even subscribing to. 😉)

- Boutique is built atop Bodega, and you can find a demo app built atop the Model View Controller Store architecture in this repo which shows you how to make an offline-ready SwiftUI app in only a few lines of code. You can read more about the thinking behind the architecture in this blog post exploring the MVCS architecture.

You may be familiar with the ``Store`` from Redux or The Composable Architecture, but unlike those frameworks you won't need to worry about adding Actions or Reducers. With this ``Store`` implementation all your data is persisted for you automatically, no additional code required. This allows you to build realtime updating apps with full offline support in an incredibly simple and straightforward manner.
You can read a high level overview of Boutique below, but Boutique is also fully documented here.
We'll go through a high level overview of the `Store` below, but the `Store` is fully documented with context, use cases, and examples here.

¹ You can have as many or as few Stores as you'd like. It may be a good strategy to have one Store for all of the notes you download in your app, but you may also want to have one Store per model-type you'd like to cache. You can even create separate stores for tests, Boutique isn't prescriptive and the choice for how you'd like to model your data is yours. You'll also notice, that's a concept from Bodega which you can read about in Bodega's StorageEngine documentation.

> **Warning** Storing binary blobs (such as images or Data) in Boutique is technically supported, but not recommended. The reason not to store images in Boutique is that storing images in Boutique's can balloon up the in-memory store, and your app's memory as a result. For similar reasons as it's not recommended to store images or binary blobs in a database, it's not recommended to store images or binary blobs in Boutique. Bodega provides a good solution for this problem, which you can read about in this tutorial.

You may have noticed that the `Store`, `StoredValue`, and `SecurelyStoredValue` are bound to the `@MainActor`. This may seem like it could cause performance issues, but I'm confident that is not the case Boutique or apps using Boutique. For additional details check out the documentation here, but I wanted to make sure you feel confident that I have deeply considered this choice, talked through the choice with Swift Concurrency experts, and have tested to make sure there are no performance implications.

As I was building v1 I noticed that people who got Boutique loved it, and people who thought it might be good but had questions grew to love it once they understood how to use it. Because of that I sought out to write a lot of documentation explaining the concepts and common use cases you'll encounter when building an iOS or macOS app. If you still have questions or suggestions I'm very open to feedback, how to contribute is discussed in the aptly named Feedback section of this readme.

Boutique is very useful on its own for building realtime offline-ready apps with just a few lines of code, but it's even more powerful when you use the Model View Controller Store architecture I've developed, demonstrated in the `NotesController` above. MVCS brings together the familiarity and simplicity of the MVC architecture you know and love with the power of a `Store`, to give your app a simple but well-defined state management and data architecture.

If you'd like to learn more about how it works you can read about the philosophy in a blog post where I explore MVCS for SwiftUI, and you can find a reference implementation of an offline-ready realtime MVCS app powered by Boutique in this repo.

We've only scratched the surface of what Boutique can do here. By leveraging Bodega's `StorageEngine`, you can build complex data pipelines that do everything from caching data to interfacing with your API server. Boutique and Bodega are more than libraries, they're a set of primitives for any data-driven application, so I suggest giving them a shot, playing with the demo app, and even building an app of your own!

That is the whole install, `pg` swapped for your database's driver: `mysql2`, `mariadb`, `better-sqlite3`, `mongodb`, `@tursodatabase/serverless` or `@libsql/client` (setup). No compiler flags and no `reflect-metadata`.

The compiler catches each of those, with no codegen: the entity classes are the schema. Try the editor on the home page.
The same queries run from the browser too: serve them over HTTP, scoped to the signed-in user by filters no `$where` can widen.

- **One API, everywhere it runs.** PostgreSQL, PGlite, CockroachDB, MySQL, MariaDB, MSSQL, SQLite, Turso, libSQL, Neon, Cloudflare D1, Bun's native SQL, and even MongoDB. The same code on Node 22.18+, Bun, Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda and Vercel, and the browser, with no native binaries on the `fetch`-based drivers.

- **Type-safe to the leaf, nothing to generate.** Every key is checked against your entity, down into populated relations and JSON/JSONB dot-paths, so `$like` on a numeric column is a compile error. No `.prisma` file, no generated client.

- **Decorators or plain data, your call.** An entity is a class with standard TC39 decorators, or plain data via `defineEntity`, its row type derived. Both are typed the same, mix in one project, and need no compiler flags or `reflect-metadata`.
- **Light.** Zero runtime dependencies and every dialect in one package, yet `uql-orm/postgres` is about 27 kB gzipped. See what we deleted to get there.

- **The hard things are built in.** Semantic and vector search, multi-tenant filters you cannot bypass by accident, soft-delete with restore, streaming, and drift checks that catch a database that no longer matches.
- **SQL when you need it.** `sql()` fits anywhere a value or a field goes, computed fields are SQL you can filter and sort on, and a migration can be plain SQL.

- **The fastest ORM.** On a full PostgreSQL round trip it adds the least over hand-written driver code of any ORM in our open-source benchmark, on Bun and Node alike. The same benchmark scores the types by compiling ordinary mistakes in each ORM's API: UQL is the only one that catches them all.

A family hub: tasks, notes, calendar, money and a shared mailbox in one place. Built for a household, not a corporation: one Docker container, one SQLite file, no external services required. Run it yourself on a home machine or a cheap VPS, or let us run it for you at neiliro.com — same code, same file per family.

`npm run db:seed` loads prices from src/db/seed/data.ts. Each entry records its official source URL and the date it was checked. Both are stored with the price (`source_url`, `checked_on`) and shown on `/prices`. Re-running the seed fills them in for prices recorded before they were stored, without changing anything already recorded. Prices apply from the date they were checked, so earlier usage has no price. Claude Haiku 5.5 (over 100,000 tokens), Gemini 2.5 Pro (over 200K) and OpenAI's gpt-5.5, gpt-5.5-pro, gpt-5.4 and gpt-5.4-pro (over 272K, from 2026-11-08) are seeded with their long-prompt tiers. Gemini 2.5 Pro is deprecated: from 2026-12-01 Google routes its requests to Gemini 3.8 Flash and bills them at Gemini 3.8 Flash rates, so its price ends there and is followed by those rates (no long-prompt tier), including their 2027-01-01 rise. Claude models are seeded with their 5-minute and 1-hour cache-write rates, Anthropic's 50% Batch API price and its $10 per 1,000 web searches. Other providers' batch and web search prices aren't seeded, because they weren't verified, so their batch usage and web searches are refused until one is added. OpenAI's audio and realtime models (gpt-audio, gpt-audio-mini, gpt-realtime-2.1 and gpt-realtime-2.1-mini) are seeded with their text and audio rates, and its image models (gpt-image-2, gpt-image-1.5 and gpt-image-1-mini) with their text and image rates, from 2026-11-07. gpt-image-2 and gpt-image-1-mini list no text output rate, so their output rate is the image output rate. Flex and fast tiers are seeded as their own prices, from the day they were checked (2026-11-07): OpenAI Flex for gpt-5.4-mini and gpt-5.4-nano, OpenAI Fast for gpt-5.4-mini, gpt-4.1 and gpt-4o-mini, and Claude Opus 5.5 fast mode ($8 / $40, with the documented cache multipliers on top). OpenAI Flex is also seeded from 2026-11-08 for gpt-5.5, gpt-5.4 and gpt-5.4-pro, with their long-context rates; tiers that publish no long-context rate (Flex for gpt-5.5-pro, Fast for gpt-5.5 and gpt-5.4) aren't, so that usage is refused rather than billed at short rates. OpenAI's gpt-6 and gpt-5.6 models are seeded from 2026-11-08 at Standard, Flex and Fast, with long-context rates, 30-minute writes as the cache-write rate, 12-hour writes as the longer-lived rate and a 50% Batch price. Re-running the seed also fills in a missing 1-hour cache-write rate, batch multiplier or web search price on existing Claude prices, and a missing end date (such as Gemini 2.5 Pro's), never changing one already recorded. Re-running the seed never overwrites existing rows, so a database seeded before cache-write rates were added keeps its old rows; reset it, or add a new row with a later `effectiveFrom`, to pick them up.

Each key has a **scope**. `ingest`, the default, sends usage, outcomes and OpenTelemetry traces. `read` (`--scope read`) reads the reporting API and can send nothing. A key does only one, so a key embedded in an app that sends usage can't be used to read your cost data. Using a key in the wrong place returns a 403 `insufficient_scope`.

`status` is `warning` at 80% and `over` at 100%. Amounts are exact decimal strings, and `usedPercent` is `null` for spend against a zero budget. With `BUDGET_ALERT_WEBHOOK_SECRET` set, an `x-cost-tracker-signature: t=<unix seconds>,v1=<hex>` header carries an HMAC-SHA256 of `<t>.<raw body>` under the secret. Compare it in constant time, and reject old timestamps to stop replays.

- **Forecast over budget** (`spend.forecast_over_budget`): a project that isn't over its monthly budget yet, but whose month-end forecast reaches it. Sent once per project, month and destination. The body has `period` (the month), `spentUsd`, `projectedUsd`, `budgetUsd` and `lastDay`.

Dimah Starter — a server-first starter for multi-tenant SaaS

- **Multi-tenant from day one.** Organizations, invitations, member roles and a platform admin panel are built and wired to Better Auth — with permission checks on every page _and_ every data read, not just in layouts.
- **Next.js 16 as it is meant to be used.** Built on Cache Components and Partial Prefetching — not an older App Router kit with a version bump — plus React 19 with the React Compiler, and Turbopack.

- **Made to be extended by AI agents.** `AGENTS.md` and the task guides in `docs/agents/` tell Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Copilot where code goes, which file to copy and how to check the result; with the Next.js MCP server connected, they can read the running app's errors too.
`cacheComponents` and `partialPrefetching` are on in `next.config.ts`, and every feature follows the model instead of working around it:

|**Cache Components** — `'use cache'`, `cacheTag`, `cacheLife`|Every list and profile read is a cache entry tagged per user or organization, e.g. the members list/manage/members/lib/get-organization-members-page.ts>)|

|**Partial Prefetching**|Links prefetch each route's App Shell, so a client navigation shows the next page's frame at once and the signed-in parts stream in. Playwright checks it with `instant()` from `@next/playwright`|
|**`updateTag`**|A Server Action expires exactly the tags it changed, and the person who acted sees fresh data in the same response — no `router.refresh()`, no client cache|
|**`refresh()` · `after()`**|Lists without a tag re-render from the action; storage cleanup runs after the response is sent|
|**Server Actions**|Every write — auth, organizations, admin, uploads — is one file under `app/action/`, mirroring its route|
|**React Compiler · Turbopack**|No hand-written `useMemo` / `useCallback`; fast dev server and builds|
The rules behind it — what to cache, which tag to expire, why sessions are never cached — are in nextjs.md.

**Want to try it?** Read MG iSmart account and session limits first, because GarageStack and the MG app cannot be signed in to the same account at once, then pick an installation option. A single `docker run` is enough to get going.

- **Directions to the car** -- Open walking directions to the car's last known location from the dashboard or the car's map marker, on OpenStreetMap or, if you prefer, Google Maps, Apple Maps or a map app on your phone. See Directions to the car.

- **Phone GPS (Dawarich)** -- Fill gaps in recorded car trips with phone locations from your own Dawarich instance. Identify trackers by their app/device ID and last-seen time; you can link multiple phones, and GarageStack uses the best match for each trip. See Phone GPS setup.

- **Trip log** -- Mark each trip as business, commute or private (commutes between your home and work are marked automatically), add notes, hide a GPS glitch, join two trips a fuel stop split, fix a route the car recorded badly on the map, and export a month or a year as a spreadsheet with the addresses and odometer readings a tax trip log (such as the Dutch *rittenregistratie*) asks for. See Trip log.

- **Dutch registration (RDW)** -- For a car with a Dutch licence plate, a dashboard card with the date the APK runs out and the days left, open recalls with what can go wrong and what the dealer does about it, and whether the car is insured, from the RDW's open data. Notifications come for a new recall, the APK a month and a week ahead, and a car with no insurance on record. Off until `RDW_ENABLED=true`; the plate, entered under Settings, is the only thing sent. See Dutch registration (RDW).

- **Homepage widget** -- A read-only API endpoint for the gethomepage.dev Custom API widget, exposing key vehicle stats at a glance, along with the APK days left, open recalls, the maintenance due next and the last trip.

- **Calendar feed** -- Subscribe to the APK expiry date, maintenance due dates and the coming climate schedules in Google Calendar, Apple Calendar, Outlook or any other calendar app. See Calendar feed.

- **Home Assistant** -- Your car appears in Home Assistant automatically through MQTT discovery, sharing GarageStack's broker and MG session instead of needing a second integration. GarageStack adds sensors of its own to the car: the APK and its days left, open recalls, the maintenance due next and the last trip. See `HOME_ASSISTANT.md`.

- **Progressive Web App (PWA)** -- Installable on mobile or desktop for a native app-like experience, complete with a home screen icon and push notification support. Where the browser allows it, GarageStack offers to install itself, and the offer can be turned down for good. It also opens without a connection, in an underground car park or away from home without your VPN: every page then shows what that device last loaded (the dashboard, statistics, the map with its routes, the trip log, charge history, maintenance and climate schedules) and says so and from when, the buttons that need the server (commands, editing, the log viewer) are hidden until it can be reached again, and the directions dialog still offers the coordinates and a `geo:` link for a map app with offline maps. The maps keep their streets too: the app keeps the map tiles it has shown (up to about 150 raster tiles and 400 basemap files, for a month), so the areas you looked at with a signal are there offline. It never downloads areas you have not looked at, which OpenStreetMap's tile policy forbids. The saved pages and the kept tiles are forgotten on signing out. Installing and push need HTTPS, see HTTPS.

- **Charging stations** -- Overlay nearby EV charging stations on the map, sourced from the Open Charge Map database. Station data is cached in the database for 7 days; on page load the map immediately shows all stations within 100 km of your car that are already cached. Markers show operational status; clicking a marker displays the station name, operator, address, and available connector types with power ratings. Requires a free OCM API key (`OPENCHARGEMAP_API_KEY`). Unlike fuel stations and service areas, charging station tiles are loaded on demand as you browse the map and are not pre-populated by the background Worker.

- **Place names** -- Trips are listed by where they went ("Zwolle to Deventer") instead of by date alone, and the dashboard's location card names the street the car is parked in. Sourced from OpenStreetMap via Nominatim -- no API key required, answers are cached in the database for 90 days, and the whole feature can be switched off under Settings > Map, or for the deployment with `GEOCODING__ENABLED=false`.

- **Snapped trip lines** -- A selected trip is drawn along the roads it was driven on rather than in straight lines between GPS fixes, which also gives a truer distance than the fixes alone. Matched against OpenStreetMap by Valhalla -- no API key required, snapped trips are cached in the database for 30 days, and it can be switched off in the map's filter panel or for the deployment with `MAPMATCHING__ENABLED=false`.

- **Themed vector basemap** -- Every map is drawn from OpenStreetMap vector tiles by MapLibre GL, in a dark or light style that follows the interface theme (or in full colour, if you prefer) and with labels in the interface language. Served by OpenFreeMap without an API key, point it at your own tile server if you prefer, and it falls back to raster tiles where WebGL is unavailable.

- **Single sign-on** -- Sign in through your own identity provider (Authentik, Authelia, Keycloak, Pocket ID, Google, and anything else speaking OpenID Connect), with optional auto-login and group or email based access restrictions. A built-in username/password login remains available for installs without a provider. See `AUTHENTICATION.md`.

Database migrations run automatically on startup and only forwards, so to go back to an older version, restore the backup you took before upgrading (see Backup and restore). A new PostgreSQL major version is never installed by an update: moving from 18 to the next one means a `pg_dump` from the old version and a restore into a fresh volume on the new one, step by step in Moving to a new PostgreSQL major version.

Without it, `docker compose up` stops with "The container name ... is already in use". Don't remove the old containers to get past that: GarageStack would start on new, empty volumes. If that already happened, see My data is gone after switching.

When a newer release is out, the footer (on a phone, the bottom of the menu) says so and links to its release notes. GarageStack asks GitHub once a day; set `UPDATE_CHECK_ENABLED=false` to stop it. Telemetry older than a year is folded into one row per quarter of an hour, so the database keeps growing, but far more slowly. Compaction cannot be undone, so take a backup first if you want to keep the raw rows. Set `TELEMETRY_FULL_DETAIL_DAYS` to change the period, or to `0` to keep every row. See Data kept over time.

Every proxy in front of the API (yours, and with Compose the frontend container) is trusted by default as long as it has a private address, so visitors are told apart for the login rate limit without further setup. The catch is that anything else on your LAN is believed the same way and could claim to be a new visitor on every sign-in attempt, so in that default sign-ins are also capped per device in front of the frontend container (30 per 5 minutes; a household behind one proxy shares that). To close the gap, list each proxy in `ForwardedHeaders__TrustedProxies__0`, `__1`, ... (see CONFIGURATION.md): then only those are believed and the extra cap is off. The frontend container is one of them, and when your proxy reaches it over a Docker network, list that network as a range (`172.18.0.0/16`) rather than single addresses, which change when a container is recreated.
